title: Retrieval & RAG
blurb: How LLMs get access to knowledge they weren't trained on. Embeddings, vector stores, hybrid search, reranking, chunking, the architecture patterns that actually work, and how to evaluate any of it.

nodes.label: Embeddings (text, multimodal)
nodes.description: Modern embedding models (text and multimodal), how to choose one, what dimensions and pooling mean, why bigger isn't always better.
nodes.doneWhen: You can pick an embedding model for a task, defend the choice, and run an A/B against an alternative.

resources.title: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB)
resources.annotation: Live leaderboard. Filter by task, language, license; the cheapest way to pick a starting model.

resources.title: Sentence-Transformers documentation
resources.annotation: The practical entry point. Pretrained models, one-line APIs, training scripts. Read the Pretrained Models page first.

resources.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning
resources.author: Kusupati et al.
resources.annotation: Matryoshka embeddings — one model, many usable dimension cutoffs. The technique behind OpenAI's truncation-friendly embeddings.

nodes.label: Vector stores
nodes.description: pgvector, FAISS, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus. ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF), filtering, hybrid storage. The right choice depends on scale and operational reality.
nodes.doneWhen: You can pick a vector store for a deployment and explain its index choice.

resources.title: pgvector
resources.annotation: Postgres extension. Often the right answer: your existing database becomes your vector store, with HNSW and filtering built in.

resources.title: Qdrant
resources.annotation: A modern open-source vector store with a strong rust core. The right choice when Postgres isn't enough but a managed service is too much.

resources.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using HNSW
resources.author: Malkov & Yashunin
resources.annotation: The HNSW paper. The index every modern vector store uses; eight pages and worth reading once.

nodes.label: Hybrid search (BM25 + vector)
nodes.description: Why BM25 still beats vector on exact-match queries, why combining the two is the practical default, score fusion (RRF).
nodes.doneWhen: You can implement BM25 + dense hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion and measure its lift.

resources.title: BM25 — Probabilistic Relevance Framework
resources.author: Robertson & Zaragoza
resources.annotation: The canonical BM25 reference. Read once; understanding it gives you the right baseline to argue against.

resources.title: Elastic — Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion
resources.annotation: The practical recipe: RRF fuses BM25 and vector scores without normalization. Two-paragraph idea; you'll use it everywhere.

nodes.label: Reranking
nodes.description: Cross-encoders, ColBERT-style late interaction, LLM rerankers. Why retrieval+rerank is almost always better than retrieval alone.
nodes.doneWhen: You can add a reranker to a retrieval pipeline and measure recall-at-k vs precision-at-k changes.

resources.title: Cohere — Rerank
resources.annotation: The most-used reranker API. The docs explain when reranking helps and how to wire it into a retrieval stack.

resources.title: ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction
resources.author: Santhanam et al.
resources.annotation: Late-interaction retrieval. The right reference when 'just a reranker' isn't enough and you want to push the retrieval stack harder.

nodes.label: Chunking strategies
nodes.description: Fixed-size, sentence, recursive, semantic, structure-aware. The most-overlooked lever in a mediocre RAG system.
nodes.doneWhen: You can run a chunking-size sweep and report which choice wins on your evaluation set.

resources.title: Chunking Strategies for LLM Applications
resources.author: Pinecone
resources.annotation: The pragmatic taxonomy: fixed-size, sentence, recursive, structure-aware. The right first read on a problem most teams underweight.

resources.title: LangChain — Text Splitters
resources.annotation: The implementations behind most production RAG splitters. Useful as a 'menu of strategies' reference even if you don't use LangChain.

nodes.label: Document parsing (PDF, HTML, OCR)
nodes.description: Where most production RAG systems lose accuracy. Layout-aware PDF parsers, HTML cleanup, OCR for scans, table extraction.
nodes.doneWhen: You can build a parser that turns a messy corpus of PDFs and HTML into clean, structured text.

resources.title: Docling — IBM
resources.annotation: An open document-parsing toolkit covering PDFs, Word, HTML, with layout-aware structure. The strongest single open answer in 2026.

resources.title: Unstructured.io
resources.annotation: The other workhorse. Wider format coverage; pragmatic for messy enterprise corpora.

nodes.label: Query reformulation & expansion
nodes.description: HyDE, multi-query, decomposition, step-back prompting. Letting the model rewrite the query before retrieval.
nodes.doneWhen: You can add a query-rewriting step to a RAG pipeline and measure its effect on retrieval quality.

resources.title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)
resources.author: Gao et al.
resources.annotation: HyDE — generate a hypothetical answer, embed that, search with it. Surprisingly strong on zero-shot retrieval.

resources.title: Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
resources.author: Zheng et al.
resources.annotation: Step-back prompting — ask a more abstract question first. The cleanest read on query reformulation by abstraction.

nodes.label: RAG architecture patterns
nodes.description: Naive RAG, modular RAG, agentic RAG, multi-hop retrieval, query routing. The decision tree from 'simplest works' to 'this case justifies complexity'.
nodes.doneWhen: You can pick the simplest RAG architecture that meets your accuracy target and defend not making it more complex.

resources.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
resources.author: Gao et al.
resources.annotation: The current canonical RAG survey. The Naive / Advanced / Modular taxonomy is the vocabulary the field uses now.

resources.title: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems & Products — Section on RAG
resources.author: Eugene Yan
resources.annotation: The pragmatic-engineer view of RAG patterns. Pair with the survey for the production-shaped angle.

nodes.label: Advanced RAG (contextual retrieval, GraphRAG)
nodes.description: Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic's chunk-prefix trick), GraphRAG (Microsoft), late-chunking, ColBERT, fine-tuned embeddings. The frontier of retrieval research that's already in production.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe Contextual Retrieval and GraphRAG and explain when each is worth the complexity.

resources.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: Prepend each chunk with model-generated context before embedding. Simple and a measured ~50% reduction in retrieval failures.

resources.title: GraphRAG — Microsoft
resources.annotation: Build a knowledge graph from the corpus, then retrieve over it. The right tool when global / connection-spanning queries dominate.

nodes.label: RAG evaluation
nodes.description: Faithfulness, context relevance, answer relevance, retrieval recall. ragas, deepeval, the LLM-as-judge approach. Eval is the difference between a RAG demo and a RAG product.
nodes.doneWhen: You have a RAG eval set, a faithfulness metric, and a regression suite that catches index drift.

resources.title: ragas — Evaluation framework for RAG pipelines
resources.annotation: Faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision, context recall. The most-used open RAG-eval toolkit.

resources.title: Evaluating RAG: A roadmap for retrievers and rerankers
resources.author: Pinecone
resources.annotation: Clear practitioner-level guide. Pair with ragas for the open-source-toolkit angle.

nodes.label: Self-RAG & corrective retrieval
nodes.description: Self-RAG (model-decided retrieval and self-critique), Corrective RAG (CRAG — verify-then-retrieve-again), agentic RAG loops. The 'when retrieval fails, fail well' patterns that push pipeline robustness past the obvious bar.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe Self-RAG's reflection tokens and CRAG's lightweight evaluator and pick the right one for a given failure mode.

resources.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
resources.author: Asai et al.
resources.annotation: The model emits reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and whether its own draft is supported. The clearest single paper for 'retrieval as a learned policy'.

resources.title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG)
resources.author: Yan et al.
resources.annotation: A lightweight evaluator grades retrieved docs and triggers a web fallback when confidence is low. Often more pragmatic than Self-RAG to ship.

resources.title: Agentic RAG (LangGraph tutorial)
resources.annotation: Worked-through example of an agentic RAG loop: grade retrieval, rewrite the query, decide to retrieve more. Useful as a code-level reference even if you don't use LangGraph.
